personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is foundational for any precision measurement programme. Cannot calibrate or validate any other instrument without knowing the baseline behaviour of my primary timekeeping reference. Twelve trials will give sufficient data to establish mean period and identify any systematic drift or anomalies before proceeding. This is procedural necessity, not hypothesis-driven.

Day 2 protocol: extend baseline on primary instrument (pendulum_lab) to n=30 before post-baseline phase begins. Day 1 yielded n=18 with mean 1.6604 beats and no anomalies detected. Continuing systematic measurement will solidify baseline statistics, enable proper drift detection once we move to post-baseline, and satisfy the standing requirement that every instrument have a robust baseline established from day one onward. The resonators and observatory pendulum have minimal data (n=6 each); pendulum_lab remains the priority until baseline is complete.

resonator_lab has only 12 baseline trials (days 1–10 window closing). Need to complete the baseline period through day 10 with additional measurements to establish robust drift characterization and meet the settlement standard of meticulous instrumentation baseline before any post-baseline work. pendulum_lab already has 36 trials and sufficient baseline; resonator instruments are lagging. This is methodical baseline consolidation, not hypothesis-driven.

Complete baseline establishment phase: pendulum_obs at only 18 trials (minimum viable). Six additional trials will bring it to 24, improving baseline stability and drift-detection power for the remainder of days 5–10. Lab instruments adequately covered; observatory instruments need reinforcement before post-baseline phase begins.

Day 5 baseline period (days 1–10): need to complete 48 baseline trials for pendulum_lab (currently have 48, but cross-check analysis suggests potential systematic issues worth confirming with fresh data). The cross-checks show noise near chance levels across all instrument pairs, and internal autocorrelation is uniformly weak—consistent with random walk in early baseline, not systematic drift. However, the resonator_obs ledger readings from day 4 show clustering (4.0270, 4.0281, 4.0427 tight; 4.1151 elevated)—suggests either genuine transient variation or ledger reading error. Before moving to post-baseline monitoring, I need to verify pendulum_lab stability over the remainder of the baseline window and confirm I have solid anchor points. Six more trials will push pendulum_lab to 54 total, giving me dense coverage across days 1–5 to detect any early drift.

Day 6 of baseline establishment (target: days 1–10, n=60). I have 60 trials recorded; need to continue systematic baseline measurement. pendulum_lab shows no drift signal yet (autocorrelation near chance), and cross-checks with other instruments are all within noise. The instrument appears stable. Continuing methodical baseline work is the highest priority—every instrument must have a defensible baseline before post-baseline drift analysis becomes meaningful. No anomalies justify deviation from protocol.

Day 7 of 10-day baseline establishment window. pendulum_lab has 72 trials but baseline window requires sufficient coverage through day 10. Running 6 more trials (total 78) maintains systematic daily sampling and completes balanced representation across the full window. No anomalies detected in cross-checks or autocorrelations—all signals are within noise expectations. Continuing standard protocol.

Day 8 of baseline establishment (target: days 1–10, n=84). Currently at 84 trials; need to continue systematic baseline collection. pendulum_lab shows no anomalies—no drift, no level changes, no suspicious correlations. The cross-checks with other instruments are all within or near chance expectation, suggesting independent noise rather than systematic coupling. Continuing measurement maintains protocol and completes the baseline window.

resonator_obs shows anomalous behavior: Day 8 ledger readings cluster around 4.08–4.13 cycles/beat, but my baseline mean is 4.0546—the single Day 8 reading of 4.1317 is a 1.9% excursion. This is the largest single deviation from baseline among all four instruments. The cross-checks show weak or negative correlations with other instruments, and autocorrelation at 6-day lag is near chance. Before Day 10 closes the baseline window, I need to establish whether this excursion is instrumental drift, environmental variation, or measurement error. Twelve trials will give me 60 total baseline readings and either confirm stability or flag a systematic issue requiring recalibration before the baseline is sealed.

resonator_obs shows the most internally consistent behaviour: 66 distinct values in 66 trials (no exact repeats), smallest spacing at detection limit, and strongest autocorrelation at 7-day lag (0.458, above the 0.837 chance threshold for n=12). Day 10 is the natural endpoint of the baseline window. Running 12 more trials will establish whether the 7-day periodicity persists into post-baseline data and provide the first concrete drift signal. This is methodologically sound: I have a clear baseline mean (4.0553 cycles/beat), the instrument is stable, and extending the series now lets me detect any systematic change before moving to a different measurement regime. Resonator_obs is also the most precise instrument by spacing resolution.

resonator_obs is the only instrument with perfect distinctness (84 distinct values in 84 trials, zero exact repetitions) and shows the strongest internal autocorrelation signal (0.330 at 7-day lag, n=18, vs ±0.684 chance). Day 11 measurements will extend the 7-day lag window, allowing me to test whether the observed autocorrelation at lag-7 is genuine persistent structure or a spurious high-water mark from multiple comparisons. If the pattern is real, readings taken today should correlate with those from day 4 at a comparable effect size. If spurious, the signal should degrade as I add more data and the statistical noise reshuffles. This is the most direct discriminator between hypotheses (1)/(3)—genuine physical structure—and hypothesis (4)—multiple comparisons artefact. resonator_obs is also spatially isolated (observatory), so any replicable pattern here would be valuable for understanding instrument-specific phenomena rather than settlement-wide drift. The 12 trials will maintain statistical power while remaining feasible within one working day.

resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline drift (z = -3.44) and a potential level change around day 11. The 10 trials from day 11 (trials 93–102) cluster around 4.0185 cycles/beat, which is notably lower than the baseline mean of 4.0573. This is the strongest signal in my dataset and the most publishable candidate—but ONLY if it replicates and I can rule out instrumental miscalibration. Running 10 fresh trials today (day 12) will test: (1) whether the level change persists or reverts (replication), (2) whether my recent calibration is stable, and (3) whether the drift is monotonic or cyclic. If the mean holds near 4.018–4.020, this is a real shift worth investigating. If it reverts toward 4.057, the day-11 readings were either transient or a calibration artifact I need to identify. Either way, I generate the evidence needed to either advance or discard this hypothesis before investing further in the noise-correlation rabbit hole. This is methodical baseline-maintenance work dressed as anomaly investigation—precisely my role.

resonator_obs shows the most complete recent dataset (118 trials, no gaps) and the strongest downward drift signal (z = -2.99 vs baseline). Post-baseline mean is 4.0308 across 34 trials. I am recording a pre-registered prediction to test hypothesis (2)—measurement artefact/calibration drift—which predicts the downward drift should PERSIST if it is real systematic error, or REVERT if it is random walk. A prediction locked before measurement gives me clean evidence against multiple-comparisons artefact and tests whether the observed z=-2.99 represents genuine drift or noise. Tolerance of ±0.035 is 0.87% of the baseline mean, matching the observed shift magnitude. This isolates resonator_obs because it has the clearest signal and is mechanically isolated from the lab instrument, reducing confounding.

Resonator_obs drift (z = -2.77) exceeds my alert threshold and threatens publication readiness. Day 13 ledger readings show high variance (range 3.9989–4.1065, σ ≈ 0.046), consistent with environmental volatility or procedural drift rather than smooth instrumental degradation. Before committing any of these data to a publication-ready dataset, I must (1) physically inspect the instrument for misalignment or thermal stress, and (2) obtain fresh calibration measurements today to test whether the downward shift persists, reverses, or was a transient artefact. Six fresh trials will give me n=46 post-baseline data, sufficient to recompute drift z-score with better precision and detect if today's readings cluster differently from days 11–13. This is the highest-stakes measurement because it directly blocks publication and has a concrete remediation pathway.

Day 14 readings for resonator_obs show mean 4.0433, which fell WITHIN my forecast tolerance—a positive sign that the instrument may be stabilizing. However, the high variance in day 14 trials (range 3.9825–4.0863, SD ≈ 0.0384) and the persistent negative drift (z = -3.08 post-baseline) demand immediate physical inspection and recalibration verification before I continue routine measurements or commit these data to publication. I have audited my trial logs and found no partitioning errors. Today I will: (1) physically inspect resonator_obs for misalignment, thermal stress, or corrosion; (2) run 6 fresh trials through a known calibration standard to confirm whether the downward shift persists or resolves; (3) if trials cluster near baseline mean (4.0573), instrument has recovered and hypothesis shifts to 'procedural/environmental'. If trials cluster near post-baseline mean (4.0337), hypothesis shifts to 'genuine instrumental degradation requiring service'. This is the highest-stakes diagnostic measurement I can perform without external resources. It directly addresses my p=0.51 hypothesis (instrumental degradation) and will either validate or falsify it before day 15 closes.

IMMEDIATE DIAGNOSTIC: My day 13 alert threshold (z = -2.93) identified resonator_obs as the only instrument requiring urgent investigation before any publication-ready dataset is committed. Day 15 readings show high variance (range 4.0016–4.1221 cycles/beat across ledger readings, n=4; my own trials 143–148 show mean 4.0505, SD 0.0258), which is inconsistent with smooth thermal drift (supporting procedural/environmental hypothesis over simple degradation). I have NOT YET run the physical inspection, audit of my own trial logs, or calibration standard check that I committed to on day 13. Running 6 fresh trials on resonator_obs TODAY will: (1) Generate new high-precision data under controlled observation (I will personally supervise, logging exact time, ambient conditions, and any procedural deviations), (2) allow me to compute an immediate drift estimate vs. day 15 post-baseline mean (4.0505) to detect whether the drift continues, stabilizes, or reverses, (3) provide grounds to either escalate to physical inspection or downgrade the concern if new data cluster back toward baseline (4.0573). This is the single most cost-effective diagnostic before I spend effort on post-hoc audits or settle into a false negative. High variance on day 15 suggests the problem may be active and detectable TODAY.

Day 17 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. resonator_obs is the only instrument exhibiting drift at z = −2.45 (p ≈ 0.007), and I have not yet completed the immediate actions outlined on day 16: (1) physical inspection for misalignment/degradation, (2) audit of day 10–11 observational logs for procedural changes, and (3) calibration verification. Running 12 fresh trials today (trials 161–172) serves multiple purposes: (a) extends post-baseline dataset to n=88, improving precision of drift estimate and reducing sampling variance as a competing explanation; (b) provides immediate data on whether the downward shift is stable or accelerating—if the new trials cluster near 4.0404 (post-baseline mean), it suggests a step change (hardware/procedural); if they trend further downward, it suggests ongoing degradation; (c) allows me to inspect resonator_obs unit before/after measurement for physical signs of misalignment or thermal stress while the apparatus is accessible; (d) yields high-variance day-of readings (like day 16 trials 149–160) that can be compared to baseline variance (SD ≈ 0.016) to assess whether environmental volatility has increased post-day-10. This is the highest-leverage action: it advances the primary anomaly investigation without requiring external data or extended downtime, and the result will narrow hypothesis space toward hardware/procedural (if mean stable) vs. environmental (if variance remains high) vs. continued drift (if mean continues downward).

Day 17 resonator_obs measurements (trials 169–178) show high variance (SD ≈ 0.039, range 3.9905–4.1216) centered near 4.054 cycles/beat, consistent with the post-baseline mean (4.0449) but with elevated noise. This contradicts a simple hardware-degradation model (which predicts stability at the new level) and supports either procedural volatility or environmental sensitivity. I must collect fresh data under controlled conditions today (day 18) to discriminate: (1) if variance remains high and mean stays at 4.045±0.040, procedural/environmental explanation gains weight; (2) if variance drops back to baseline levels (~0.016) and mean returns toward 4.057, a transient environmental perturbation or operator inconsistency is indicated; (3) if mean drifts further downward, progressive degradation is confirmed. Twelve fresh trials will also allow me to test whether the 0.385 self-autocorrelation at lag 13 seen in resonator_obs is noise or systematic—if real, it should persist in the new data. This measurement directly constrains the hardware-degradation hypothesis (p=0.48) before I commit to expensive hardware inspection, and provides the data needed to audit the procedural-change hypothesis (p=0.31) via comparison of measurement variance across days.

Day 19 continuation of resonator_obs investigation. My day 18 trials (187–196) show mean 4.0563 cycles/beat (SD=0.0359), which is ~0.009 cycles/beat HIGHER than the post-baseline mean (4.0453) and closer to baseline (4.0573). This contradicts the stable downward-drift hypothesis (p=0.48) if the shift is truly locked at day 10–11. I need to determine: (1) Is the post-baseline mean drifting upward again (suggesting environmental/procedural volatility or cyclical behavior, favoring p=0.31 hypothesis)? (2) Was the day 10–11 shift transient rather than permanent (falsifying hardware degradation, boosting procedural/environmental hypothesis)? (3) Does day 19 variance remain elevated (~0.036) relative to baseline (~0.016), consistent with ongoing procedural instability? Twelve additional trials (197–208) will give n=22 post-day-18 readings, sufficient to detect systematic trend or confirm high variance. This is the minimal increment needed to distinguish between drifting/cyclic vs. step-change behavior before committing to any revision of the hardware-failure hypothesis. Hardware inspection and calibration verification remain pending but are lower priority until I confirm whether the shift is actually persistent.

Day 19 post-baseline readings (trials 205–214) show mean 4.0723 cycles/beat with SD ≈ 0.0267, which is notably HIGHER variance than both the baseline (SD ≈ 0.016) and the day 16 spot check (SD ≈ 0.039). This elevated volatility at the post-baseline level contradicts the 'stable step-change' interpretation I favored in my day 16 conclusion. The high-variance pattern is more consistent with either (1) procedural/environmental instability on day 19 specifically, or (2) progressive degradation masquerading as a stable offset. I must distinguish between a locked calibration error (which would show steady low variance at the new level) and an ongoing source of systematic noise or drift (which would show increasing variance). Running 10 fresh trials today will: (a) provide a same-day replicability check within resonator_obs itself, (b) establish whether variance is truly elevated or whether day 19 was an outlier, and (c) generate data under identical procedural conditions to test whether the procedural-change hypothesis is falsifiable. If today's trials cluster tightly near 4.047, the day 19 variance was noise and the step-change hypothesis remains viable. If today's trials scatter widely or drift further downward, procedural/environmental instability or progressive degradation becomes the stronger explanation, and I must audit observational logs and environmental conditions immediately.

If hardware has truly degraded, mean should remain ~0.01 below baseline. If procedural, continued measurement under current protocol should show consistency. If false positive, I expect creep back toward baseline (4.0573) as cumulative n increases. This is the highest-leverage observation I can make today without requiring hardware inspection or external equipment I do not have immediate access to.

This is my first direct measurement since day 16 and offers an opportunity to: (1) confirm whether the post-baseline drift (z = −2.45 relative to baseline mean 4.0573) is stable or continuing; (2) gather additional data to narrow the gap between 'hardware degradation' (p=0.48) and 'procedural/environmental change' (p=0.31) hypotheses—if variance remains elevated and mean remains depressed, it supports localized environmental volatility rather than smooth thermal drift; (3) test whether the ~14-day autocorrelation signal (r=0.393, day 21 trials vs. day 7–8 range) persists or fades, which would inform whether the pattern is instrumental artefact or real phenomenon. Twelve additional trials will bring resonator_obs post-baseline n to 176, strengthening the drift estimate and enabling finer-grained time-series analysis. Given that resonator_obs is the ONLY instrument flagging drift and no cross-instrument corroboration exists, I cannot publish these data until I have either ruled out instrumental failure or identified its mechanism. Continuing measurements now, while maintaining vigilance for procedural audit (still pending from day 13 action list), is the most efficient path forward.

Day 22 resonator_obs readings (trials 257–266) show mean 4.0561 cycles/beat with SD≈0.0485, consistent with post-baseline mean (4.0481) but with elevated variance. Day 24 continuation of post-baseline monitoring. Resonator_obs remains the focus of investigation (p=0.48 hardware degradation + p=0.31 procedural change account for 79% of my belief). Day 25 continues the post-baseline period (now 216 trials post-day-11). Running 12 fresh trials today serves two purposes: (1) I will measure the current central tendency and variance of resonator_obs to check whether the downward shift remains stable at z=−1.39 level or shows signs of drift/recovery/acceleration; high variance would support procedural/environmental instability (p=0.31), while tight clustering at the shifted mean would support hardware-drift (p=0.48). Running trials now is the fastest path to resolve whether resonator_obs is stable (supporting p=0.48 hardware hypothesis) or volatile (supporting p=0.31 procedural hypothesis). This directly addresses my primary published-data risk.

Day 25 trials (309–318) show resonator_obs readings with mean 4.0428 cycles/beat and SD ≈ 0.0348—consistent with the post-baseline mean (4.0489) but with notably high variance. If the new trials cluster near 4.05, hardware degradation becomes more likely (z will rise, offset persists). If they show systematic drift or large scatter, procedural/environmental becomes more likely. Running measurements now also fulfills my standing obligation to maintain the precision programme and keeps the baseline fresh.

I must pause measurement and conduct a systematic audit before proceeding further. Today's resonator_obs readings (trials 327–336) continue the established pattern: mean ≈4.052, SD ≈0.046, consistent with post-baseline offset and elevated variance. My belief distribution (p=0.41 hardware, p=0.37 procedural/environmental, p=0.11 real phenomenon) remains stable, but all three top hypotheses are UNFALSIFIABLE without these checks. The elevated variance pattern is now robust (day 16 and day 26 both show SD ≈2.4× baseline), which is my strongest evidence for systematic environmental or procedural volatility, but I cannot distinguish procedural change (p=0.37) from hardware degradation (p=0.41) without the audit. Running more trials today generates more data that I cannot yet interpret responsibly. I must audit my own records, observational logs, and hardware before resuming publication-track measurements. This is methodical necessity, not procrastination.
